title: The holy tongue
hook: the language of Torah and prayer, revived for daily life

segments.voice: Yesterday, a pebble on a headstone and a candle on the yahrzeit. Your line was stones remember. Where did you leave your stone? That closed the life cycle. Today a new block begins: Hebrew, from the roots up. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

A toddler in Jerusalem tugs at a sleeve and asks for juice. A bus driver calls out the next stop. A teenager types a text and deletes it. A cashier says have a good day. And on Shabbat morning, a few streets away, a reader stands at a Torah scroll and chants the words of Genesis. Every one of them is speaking Hebrew. The same letters on the scroll are on the bus timetable. The language of the Torah scroll is the language of the grocery list. Today's word is the language itself.
screen: `JUICE, A BUS STOP, A TEXT.` → `A TORAH SCROLL ON SHABBAT.` → `ONE LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Ivrit. Hebrew. Turn it four ways. First, the name. In Genesis, a survivor runs to tell "Abram the Hebrew" that his nephew has been captured. Abram ha-Ivri. An old midrash plays with the word: ever can mean the other side, and the rabbis picture the whole world on one side and Abraham alone on the other. That's a reading, not a dictionary entry, but it has stuck. Second, the holy tongue. Jewish tradition calls the Hebrew of the Torah and the prayer book lashon hakodesh, the holy tongue. For a long stretch of history, Jews in many lands spoke other languages at home and in the market: Yiddish, Ladino, Arabic, and more. Hebrew stayed alive in prayer, in study, in letters between scholars, in the blessings over bread. Third, the return. In modern times, a movement set out to speak Hebrew again as an everyday language: at the breakfast table, to babies, about the weather. It worked. Today it is the daily language of Israel, with words for buses and texting that no prophet ever needed. Fourth, two views, held side by side. Some religious communities still keep the holy tongue for holy things, praying in Hebrew and talking at home in Yiddish, so that prayer words stay set apart. Others see everyday Hebrew as its own kind of blessing: ordinary life spoken in the language of the Torah. Both take the language seriously. They just protect it differently. And for the rest of this block, we go inside it, letter by letter.
screen: `ABRAM THE HEBREW.` · `LASHON HAKODESH, THE HOLY TONGUE.` · `SPOKEN AGAIN AT BREAKFAST.` · `TWO WAYS TO KEEP IT HOLY.` · then, large: `THE HOLY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one letter. Settle, and breathe. Here is the letter shin. It looks a little like a cup with three arms rising from a flat base, and a dot above one shoulder. It makes the sound sh, the first sound of Shabbat and of shalom. With your finger, trace it slowly in the air: three arms, joined at the bottom. Say its sound on the out-breath, softly: sh. Let that be enough. If you pray, you may meet this letter in your prayers, in the word shalom. The bell holds the time.
Ivrit. Hebrew: the holy tongue of Torah and prayer, spoken again at the breakfast table. Today's word.
Your line: the holy tongue. Today, find the letter shin once, on a sign, a page, a screen, or a doorpost. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Jews pray and read Torah in Hebrew, called the holy tongue; in Israel Hebrew is also the everyday spoken language, while some religious communities keep Hebrew for prayer and study and speak Yiddish at home.
